archetype.name: Game Manager (veteran bridge starter)
archetype.definition: A 34-year-old, 11th-year passer who wins underneath and in the 10-19 yard window, keeps sacks and fumbles down, and keeps an offense on schedule rather than tilting games, now holding the Ravens job until Lamar Jackson returns.

report.headline: A volume-steady bridge starter whose drives die on third down and in close games.
report.take:
Jacoby Brissett has spent a decade as the quarterback teams call when the plan breaks, and his career line reads that way: EPA per play anywhere from -0.151 (2024) to 0.111 (2022), completion rates in the low 60s, a passer who is rarely the reason you lose big and rarely the reason you win close. Most of this season's line was built with Trey McBride and Michael Wilson as his top two targets. He is now Baltimore's QB1, with Jackson on injured reserve after thumb surgery and a hoped-for return in Week 16.

The engine is volume and the short-to-middle game. He throws 39.1 times a game, which is why 233.5 yards a game ranks 16th while his 5.97 yards per attempt ranks 43rd. His average throw is 7.72 air yards and lands about a yard short of the sticks, so he moves the ball in small pieces. The 10-19 yard window is where he earns his keep: 0.262 EPA per attempt, adding up to +20.7. Throws behind the line cost -14.4, and the deep ball barely works (25.6% completions, 3 interceptions on 39 attempts). His -1.12 CPOE is basically league-average accuracy, and his 12.5% bad-throw rate is cleaner than last year's 16.7%.

His overall efficiency, -0.032 EPA per dropback against a league average of -0.027, looks harmless, but the game-state split shows the problem. Trailing by nine or more he is excellent: 0.142 EPA per play, +22.6 total, a 4.8 CPOE. Within one score he falls to -0.188, a -45.1 hole, and 8 of his 9 interceptions came there. Close fourth quarters are worse, at -0.489. Third down is the same story: -0.319 EPA, a 31.3% conversion rate, no touchdowns and five picks. When defenses must stop the short game, he doesn't have a second answer. The garbage-time production props up his yardage and fantasy line more than it helps his teams.

The touchdowns have dried up. His 2.8% TD rate ranks 43rd, and over the last five games it is 1.0%, with two scores. Last year's 23 touchdowns look like the outlier when set against his 2017-2024 seasons. Baltimore gives him a middling setting: 18th in offensive EPA, a decent run game (13th), and a line that allows hits at the 24th-ranked rate. Expect 220-260 yards on heavy attempts, about one touchdown, and an interception risk that rises in tight games, for a window that probably closes when Jackson is cleared.

strengths.title: Earns his EPA between 10 and 19 yards
strengths.body: The intermediate window carries his whole passing game: 0.262 EPA per attempt and a 54.4% success rate, with the middle of the field also positive. This is a skill he has shown in better seasons such as 2022, not a fluke. It holds as long as he has a reliable middle-of-field target, and Zay Flowers' early numbers with him are promising on a small sample.

strengths.title: Avoids sacks and fumbles
strengths.body: His sack rate is 5.6%, 14th of 55 and well under the league's 7.8%. He turns only 22.1% of pressures into sacks, which ranks 8th, and has lost no fumbles. That fits his career: pressure-to-sack ranked 9th in 2019 and 12th in 2022. He is a big, patient pocket passer who gets the ball out or away, and that trait should travel to any roster.

strengths.title: Volume keeps the yards coming
strengths.body: At 39.1 attempts a game he ranks 16th in yards per game despite a bottom-tier yards per attempt. He is on a 3,970-yard pace. Over the last five games he has averaged 245 yards, a little above his season mark. As a likely underdog in most games, the volume should hold.

concerns.title: Third downs and one-score games
concerns.body: On third down he posts -0.319 EPA with a 31.3% conversion rate, no touchdowns and five interceptions. Within one score his EPA falls to -0.188, a -45.1 total. This is a real limitation, not role noise. When defenses take away the underneath stuff, he lacks a vertical answer and forces throws. His career-long middling win rates suggest this is who he is.

concerns.title: Touchdowns have dried up
concerns.body: His 2.8% TD rate ranks 43rd. In the last five games it is 1.0%, and his touchdowns per game are down 0.82 from last year. In the red zone his completion rate is 13.2 points under expected, so the 10 touchdowns there came despite inaccurate work. Some bounce-back is likely as the volume returns, but his career baseline is a modest scorer.

concerns.title: Garbage time inflates the line
concerns.body: Trailing by nine or more he plays like an above-average starter, at 0.142 EPA and a 4.8 CPOE against soft, prevent-style coverage. That cushions his season totals and fantasy points. It also means his production is partly a byproduct of his teams losing, so the stats overstate his ability to win games.

trend.note: The game log swings hard, from +8.2 EPA in Week 3 to -15 in Week 4. Since Week 6 the efficiency has slipped to -0.053 per dropback and the touchdowns have nearly vanished. The rough patch bottomed out in Week 8 (58% of snaps, 58.6% pressured), and the last two games were steadier, with yards up and EPA positive.

nextGame.headline: Pass-funnel Texans offer yards, but their pass rush sacks often
nextGame.body:
Houston is a 6.5-point home favorite, and their offense ranks 8th in passing EPA, so the likely script has Brissett trailing and throwing a lot. That is the state where he has been at his best. The Texans also funnel teams to the air (pass rate 3.1 points over norm, 6th), allow 262.5 passing yards a game (25th), and give up explosive passes at the second-worst rate. Against that, they rank 6th in success rate and 3rd in sack rate. That combination punishes the stalled third downs where he already struggles, behind a Baltimore line that ranks 24th at preventing hits.

Danielle Hunter, a 76%-snap edge rusher, is out, and DT Sheldon Rankins is questionable. That takes real heat off a passer whose game depends on time to work the middle. On Houston's offense, WR Marvin Harrison Jr. is out, and RB Woody Marks is out on the report with a hopeful note, which could slow the Texans' scoring a little. Brissett is listed active after an old Week 9 missed practice.

keyMatchups.title: Texans pass rush minus Hunter
keyMatchups.body: Houston sacks quarterbacks on 8.9% of dropbacks, third-most, and Baltimore's line ranks 24th in hit rate. Hunter's absence should soften that. Brissett's low pressure-to-sack rate is the best matchup he has here. If the edge rush still gets home, third-and-long becomes his worst situation again.

keyMatchups.title: WR2 is the soft spot
keyMatchups.body: Houston holds tight ends 3.0 PPR under their average (3rd) and lets second receivers score 4.0 over theirs (30th). It also allows 0.51 EPA a target to WR2s. His intermediate game should look outside the tight end, toward the secondary option opposite the top receiver.

keyMatchups.title: Explosive plays he rarely creates
keyMatchups.body: Houston allows explosive passes at the 31st-ranked rate, but Brissett completes only 25.6% of his 20-plus-yard throws, with a -11 CPOE there. The leak only matters if he hits a couple of shots. More likely the big plays come after the catch on the short and intermediate throws he already makes.

nextGame.watch: Watch his third-down conversions and whether he can sustain drives without Hunter's pressure; if he stays a 30% converter, the yards come late and empty.

restOfSeason.body:
Brissett's window looks like about four starts, with Jackson's estimated return date of December 27 lining up with a hoped-for Week 16 comeback. The yardage is the stable part: heavy attempts, a usable intermediate game and a likely underdog script should keep him around 220-260 yards a game. The touchdown rate should drift up from its recent 1.0% toward his career norm, since red-zone volume eventually converts. Even so, roughly one touchdown a game is the honest expectation, not last year's near-two.

The interceptions are the part that won't regress much. They come from forced throws on third down and in one-score games, a long-running trait rather than bad luck. A run-capable Baltimore offense (13th in rushing EPA) could cut his volume when games stay close. If so, expect fewer garbage-time yards and fantasy outings in the 10-15 point range.
swingFactors: Timing of Lamar Jackson's return from thumb surgery
How often Baltimore trails by two scores
Whether Zay Flowers becomes his steady middle-of-field target

confidence.note: Ten-game sample with a clear career baseline, but mostly built on another roster before his move to Baltimore.
